briefing.headline: Read it. Don't write it.
body: Every app Claude builds for you will be JavaScript. When Claude explains what it did, writes a comment, names a function, or reports an error — that's JavaScript. You don't need to write it fluently. You need to read it well enough to know when it's wrong, ask the right follow-up, and give Claude useful constraints instead of vague directions.

This module is not JavaScript 101. It's the subset that matters for directing: variables, functions, objects, arrays, and async/await. Those five concepts cover ~80% of what you'll encounter in the code Claude ships. The rest you'll look up as needed.

reference.title: Variables: const vs let
reference.content:
const name = 'Riffle';      // can't be reassigned
let count = 0;              // can be reassigned
count = count + 1;          // fine
name = 'Other';             // TypeError — const is final

reference.title: Function forms
Objects and arrays
async/await in plain English
reference.content: JavaScript runs one thing at a time, but some operations (API calls, file reads) take a while. async/await lets code pause and wait for a result without blocking everything else. A function marked async always returns a Promise. await inside it pauses that function until the Promise resolves. If the Promise rejects (error), try/catch catches it.

reference.title: async/await pattern
Array methods you'll see constantly
reference.content:
const catches = [14, 18, 22, 11];

catches.map(len => len * 2.54);   // convert to cm — new array
catches.filter(len => len > 15);  // only over 15" — new array
catches.find(len => len > 20);    // first over 20" — single value
catches.forEach(len => console.log(len)); // loop, no return

reference.title: "undefined is not a function"
reference.content: You're calling something as a function that isn't one. Common cause: a typo in the function name, or calling a method on an object before it's been assigned. Ask Claude to add a console.log before the failing line to see what you actually have.

reference.title: "Cannot read properties of undefined"
reference.content: You're trying to access a property (e.g. data.catches) on something that is undefined. Usually means an API call returned nothing, a variable wasn't initialized, or you're accessing a nested property too early. Add console.log(data) before the failing line.

completion.headline: M4 complete.
completion.body: You can read JavaScript — variables, functions, objects, arrays, async/await. That's enough to direct Claude with precision and know when the code it ships is wrong. Next up: M5 — Node.js & npm.

steps.title: Open a scratch file
steps.body: This module is read-first, run-second. You're not building anything — you're running small experiments to see how JavaScript actually behaves. Create a file to work in.
steps.verify: ls shows scratch.js. Open it in VS Code with code ..

commandNotes.what: Creates the folder and immediately moves into it. The && runs the second command only if the first succeeds.
commandNotes.when: Any time you're creating a folder you immediately want to work in. Same pattern works for project setup.

whenYoullReachForThis: Creating a quick scratch folder to test a Claude-generated snippet before adding it to a real project
Isolating a small piece of behavior — does this function return what I think it returns? — without touching your actual codebase
Prototyping a data transformation before Claude wires it into the app

steps.title: Variables: const and let
steps.body: JavaScript has two variable types you'll use: const for values that don't change, let for values that do. You'll see const everywhere in modern code — most variables don't need to change after they're set. The third option, var, is old; Claude won't use it and neither should you.
steps.tryCue: Paste into scratch.js and run with node scratch.js.

commandNotes.what: Runs the file with Node.js — JavaScript outside the browser. Every line executes top to bottom.
commandNotes.when: Testing any .js file locally. The primary way you'll verify Claude's code before wiring it into an app.

commandNotes.what: Prints a value to the terminal. The most basic debugging tool in JavaScript.
commandNotes.when: Whenever you want to see what a variable actually contains mid-execution. You'll use this constantly — even experienced engineers do.

steps.verify: Terminal shows Rainbow Trout, 0, 1. Uncomment the last line and run again — you get a TypeError: Assignment to constant variable.
whenYoullReachForThis: Reading Claude's code and seeing const apiKey = ... — that value won't change anywhere in the function
Spotting a bug where a value should change but was declared const — tell Claude to switch it to let
Understanding why Claude named something with all-caps (const MAX_RETRIES = 3) — convention for constants that are configuration values

steps.title: Functions: declaration and arrow
steps.body: Functions are reusable named chunks of logic. Claude writes them two ways: the function keyword (older, explicit) and arrow functions (=>, more common in modern code). They behave nearly identically for your purposes — when you're reading code, they're interchangeable. The arrow form is shorter and you'll see it far more often.
steps.tryCue: Replace scratch.js contents with this. Run it.

commandNotes.what: Sends a value back to whoever called the function. Without return, the function returns undefined.
commandNotes.when: If Claude's function produces no output when you expected one, return is often the missing piece.

commandNotes.what: When an arrow function body is a single expression without curly braces, the result is returned automatically.
commandNotes.when: You'll see this on short transformation functions — items.map(item => item.name). No curly braces, no return keyword.

steps.verify: Terminal shows three formatted catch strings, one per function style.
whenYoullReachForThis: Claude generates a helper function and you want to understand what it takes in and what it gives back — find the parameters and the return
A function produces undefined — check whether there's a return statement
Asking Claude to extract repeated logic into a function — tell it the input values and the expected output and let it pick the style

steps.title: Objects
steps.body: Objects are collections of named values — the main way JavaScript organizes data. Almost everything Claude builds uses objects: an API response, a row of catch data, a config block. The key skill is reading them: finding a property, spotting a nested object, knowing what's optional vs. required.

commandNotes.what: Access a property by name. The most common way to read object data.
commandNotes.when: Anytime you're pulling a specific field out of an object — response.data, user.email, catch.length.

commandNotes.what: Chain dot notation for nested objects. Each . goes one level deeper.
commandNotes.when: API responses are frequently nested — response.data.catches[0].species. If this chain fails, one of the intermediate values is undefined.

commandNotes.what: Returns an array of all property names on the object.
commandNotes.when: Exploring an unfamiliar object — paste it into a scratch file and console.log(Object.keys(thing)) to see what's available.

steps.verify: Terminal shows Rainbow Trout, Yakima, Elk Hair Caddis, 52, and an array of all property names.
whenYoullReachForThis: Claude's code accesses response.data.items and fails — one of those properties doesn't exist, and you need to log the intermediate value to find out which
Asking Claude to add a field to an existing data structure — describe the object shape and where the new field fits
Reading a Claude-generated config object — understanding which keys are required vs. optional based on how they're used

steps.title: Arrays and the three methods
steps.body: Arrays are ordered lists. You'll use them everywhere: a list of catches, a set of API results, a batch of transcript lines. Three array methods cover most of what you'll encounter in Claude's code: map (transform every item), filter (keep some items), find (get one item). The fourth — forEach — just loops.
steps.tryCue: Replace scratch.js with this. Run it. Read each output before moving on.

commandNotes.what: Returns a new array where each item is the result of the callback. Original array untouched.
commandNotes.when: Transforming a list of API results into display strings, converting units, pulling one field out of each object.

commandNotes.what: Returns a new array containing only items where the callback returns true.
commandNotes.when: Removing items below a threshold, filtering by a category, hiding already-confirmed catches from the unreviewed list.

commandNotes.what: Returns the first matching item, not an array. Returns undefined if nothing matches.
commandNotes.when: Looking up a single record by ID or condition. If it might not exist, check for undefined before accessing properties.

steps.verify: Terminal shows four sections: a labels array, two keeper objects, one big-fish object, and all four catches formatted individually.
whenYoullReachForThis: Claude maps over an API response and you get undefined in the output — the property name inside the callback is wrong
The app is showing all catches instead of just today's — Claude needs a filter() on the date field
Asking Claude to find a specific catch in a list — that's a find(), give Claude the field and the matching value

steps.title: async/await: the one concept that unlocks APIs
steps.body: Almost everything interesting in an app — fetching data, calling Claude, reading a file — takes time. JavaScript handles that with async/await. An async function can pause at any await line until a result arrives. Without it, you'd try to use data before it exists. With it, code reads top-to-bottom like normal. The tricky part: forgetting await gives you a Promise object instead of the value you expected — and it won't error, it'll just behave wrong.
steps.tryCue: Replace scratch.js with this. Run it and watch the order of output.

commandNotes.what: Marks a function as asynchronous — it can use await inside and always returns a Promise.
commandNotes.when: Any function that makes an API call, reads a file, or calls another async function needs to be async. Forgetting this gives you a syntax error when you try to use await inside.

commandNotes.what: Pauses execution at this line until the Promise resolves. Gives you the value, not the Promise.
commandNotes.when: Every time you call a function that returns a Promise — API calls, fetch(), Claude SDK calls, file operations. Skipping await is the most common async bug.

commandNotes.what: Catches errors from awaited operations. Without it, a failed API call crashes silently.
commandNotes.when: Wrapping any await that could fail — network calls, file reads, external APIs. Claude should always generate this; if it doesn't, ask for it.

steps.verify: Output shows Start, then Fetching species 1, then a 500ms pause, then Got: { id: 1, species: ... }, then the Promise object (not data) for the missing-await case.
steps.trouble: If you see SyntaxError: await is only valid in async functions — you used await outside an async function. Wrap the calling code in async function main() { ... } and call main().
whenYoullReachForThis: Claude's API call returns a Promise object instead of data — a missing await; ask Claude to add it
The app shows undefined where a fetched value should be — the render happened before the async call finished; Claude needs to handle the loading state
Reading any Claude-generated function that calls the Anthropic SDK — every client.messages.create() is async and needs await

steps.title: try/catch: error handling
steps.body: try/catch is how JavaScript handles errors without crashing. The try block runs normally; if anything throws an error, execution jumps to catch. In production apps, every async operation should be wrapped in one. If Claude generates code without try/catch around API calls, ask for it — an unhandled network error will silently break the app.
steps.tryCue: Replace scratch.js with this. Run it twice — once as-is, once with shouldFail = true.

commandNotes.what: Receives the thrown error object. error.message is the human-readable description.
commandNotes.when: When diagnosing a Claude-generated error in production — log error.message and error.stack for full context.

commandNotes.what: Runs whether or not an error occurred. Good for cleanup — closing a connection, setting a loading state to false.
commandNotes.when: Ask Claude to add a finally block when you need to guarantee something happens — resetting a spinner, logging completion.

steps.verify: First run: Success: { species: 'Brown Trout', length: 16 } plus the finally line. Second run (shouldFail = true): Something went wrong: Network timeout plus the finally line.
whenYoullReachForThis: Claude's code has no error handling around an API call — ask it to wrap the await in try/catch with a useful error message
App crashes silently when the network is slow — add try/catch and log the error to understand what's happening
A loading spinner never goes away — finally block with setLoading(false) is the fix

steps.title: Read real Claude-generated code
steps.body: Everything you've done so far was synthetic. Now apply it. Ask Claude to generate a small function — something Riffle-adjacent — and read the output carefully. The goal isn't to modify it; it's to be able to explain what each line does.
steps.tryCue: Open Claude. Paste this prompt exactly.
steps.code: Write a JavaScript function called parseFishingEntry that takes a string like "Caught a 16-inch brown trout on an elk hair caddis at the upper Yakima" and returns an object with fields: species, length, fly, and location. Use regex or string parsing — whatever is simpler. Include try/catch. No explanation needed, just the function.
notes: Read the function line by line.
Find: the parameters, the return value, any await, any try/catch.
Paste it into scratch.js and call it with a few test strings.
If something doesn't behave as expected, console.log the intermediate values.
steps.verify: You can explain, in plain English, what each section of the function does. You called it with at least two inputs and got back an object.
whenYoullReachForThis: Any time Claude generates a non-trivial function — read it before running it; a 2-minute read saves a 20-minute debug
Building Riffle's transcript parsing — Claude will write the parsing logic; you direct the input format and the expected output shape
Code review with a collaborator — you need to be able to say "this function takes X and returns Y" without reading it aloud for the first time

steps.title: Clean up
steps.body: Delete the scratch folder. You won't need it again.
